To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) The CRLB is proportional to 1/(PRI2 K3) and (2) the CRLB is inversely proportional to the product of the signal to noise ratio of each pulse and the sampling frequency.
the CRLBs are proportional to 1/(PRI2 K3 SNR) and are independent of pulse shape and modulation.

The CRLB for the frequency estimation of coherent pulse trains depends on the pulse on time, the number of pulses, the variance of pulse times (or equivalently the variance of the PRI), the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and sampling frequency.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of estimating the Doppler shift of a coherent pulse-train signal received by a moving antenna.
the development of a novel method for estimating the location of a target in the presence of noise.
the estimation of the frequency of coherent pulse train passivity intercepted at a moving radar.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CRLBs derived herein provide the best possible estimates of the frequency, and thus location, of a radar.
the CRLBs are very small and are not likely to be of practical significance.
the CRLBs derived herein are a useful tool to assess the potential of frequency estimation for location of a coherent pulse radar.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
for a coherent pulse train with K pulses of length Tp and PRI Tp, the CRLB is approximately equal to (Tp2/Ts)2/(2K3) where Ts is the sampling interval.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CRLBs are not as good as previously believed and are much more dependent on the number of pulses than previously thought.
the CRLBs are much lower than previously thought and that the CRLBS can be used to assess the potential accuracy of location algorithms.
the CRLBs of the frequency estimates are inversely proportional to the product of signal-to-noise ratio and sampling frequency.
